items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. Call opened 'Hi, this is Daniel with Einstein moving, how can I help you?' and went straight into date availability, then into a long inventory walk with no roadmap and no timeframe — the customer was never told this would take 10-15 minutes or what the sequence would be, which matters on a call that ran 18 minutes and touched three locations.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Packing services never raised — the single biggest miss on the call. The customer's second sentence was 'a house that needs to be packed up.' Daniel never asked whether she wanted Einstein to pack, never quoted packing (same hourly rate + materials), and never built packing time into the 7-8 hour estimate. A stated need was left on the table and the estimate may now be structurally short if she expects the crew to pack.
Disassembly / reassembly never mentioned as included, despite three desks, garage shelves, an inversion table and a 'Pilates equipment piece' in the inventory — all classic breakdown items.
Assembly/disassembly also missing from the estimate variables, so she has no idea whether the crew breaking down desks and shelves is inside or outside the 7-8 hours.

Drive time between stops never explained. This is a three-stop job (house + shed to CubeSmart on South Congress, office ~9 miles to 1512 West ... Lane) and he correctly said 'you do not pay for us to drive out there or to drive back from this locations' — but never said the inter-stop drive IS on the clock. That is a billing-surprise risk on exactly the job type where it bites.

On-Time Guarantee named but the mechanic was left out. He said 'we do have an on time guarantee that just says we aren't going to be hours and hours late on any given date and then we're not just gonna cancel day off' — the actual promise, that Einstein starts discounting immediately if the window is missed, was never stated. Counted as a hit on the bullet, but it landed as a reassurance rather than a guarantee.

Save Your Ass prep speech not delivered. He gestured at it — 'if you really hone in kind of clear communication that does help be at four hours three to four hours for the load up' and 'if the inventory is changing or if he wants to place a certain way all of those are kind of efficiency factors' — but gave her zero actions to take before move day. No consolidation examples, no 'take a carload,' nothing. This on a job that is a loose shed, garage shelves, Christmas boxes, a container of cleaning supplies and patio furniture — the highest-yield prep-speech inventory you can get.

No volume equivalent used to help her picture the load. 'We got the two bedroom kind of equivalent' is a size shorthand, not the school-bus / truck-load reference the rubric asks for, and she had just told him 'I have no idea what the square footage is.'

Walk distance collected but never explained as a time driver. He asked 'is the unit pretty close to the elevator on the third floor or how long we walk, would you say' and she answered 'it's in the middle' — then he priced the storage leg at 1.5-2 hours without ever connecting the walk to that number.

Parking / loading access never asked at the office destination or at the origin. Gate codes only came up because the customer volunteered them ('the only gate codes we potentially would have to worry about it at the storage unit').

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections.' Closest he got was 'just let us know if there's any major changes or questions, a quick email or phone call' — partial credit, but she was never asked to verify the inventory, addresses or date in writing. On a three-stop move built entirely from a verbal inventory, written verification is the control that protects the estimate.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' — he closed on his own summary instead.
Hours and how to reach us never given.
Customer's name used twice ('Sorry, you cut out there Stephanie one more time' and 'So, Stephanie and then Renee R-E-N-E-A you said') — short of the 3+ standard.

Repeat-customer moment squandered. She said 'I've used you before' and the entire response was 'Oh, nice, okay, gotcha.' No thank-you, no 'welcome back,' no pull of her prior job to speed up the inventory or sanity-check the estimate.
Insurance explanation stopped short of the 60c/lb baseline — the $2,000 No Worries coverage was explained well, but without the legal-minimum contrast it loses most of its punch.
top_strength: The inventory build was genuinely excellent and it is the reason this call scored where it did. Faced with a customer who said 'I have no idea what the square footage is,' Daniel reframed correctly on the spot — 'We are just time based. So yeah, square footage isn't really super pertinent it's just really what's coming with us, that's important. So, if you want to just walk through an inventory so I can kind of get an idea' — then organized the whole thing by location out loud: 'I'm just trying to split it up so it's a little bit clear.' He kept probing where a weaker rep would have moved on: he chased the outdoor table down to its material and height ('was it like a rod iron kind of, sort of thing or any stone tables'), separated shed from office from house, caught the patio himself ('was there any patio stuff at all outside of the shed' — she answered 'Uh-oh good call'), and pre-empted a real damage risk on the filing cabinets: 'do you know of any of them having like Dinky wheels on them that my break with being moved... I can also make sure the truck is a lift gate too just in case any of them are really heavy.' The clock section was perfect and the estimate was then built segment by segment rather than as one hand-waved number — 3-4 hours load, 1.5-2 hours at the third-floor storage unit, 1.5-2 hours unload, 'seven to eight hour range,' with correct math on both ends ($1,664 at eight hours, $1,456 at seven). He also caught a scheduling trap himself: when she said Wednesday, he flagged 'Wednesday is actually the only day of the month that we're going to be closed. That's our company training day,' and steered her to Tuesday the 8th. He booked the job — 'we don't need to send the quote to kind of look over as well as hold the date for the Tuesday the eighth' / 'Yes please' — while also stacking the no-friction pitch (no deposit, no rescheduling fee, no cancellation fee, payment at the end by card reader).
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix is packing, and it is worth real money on this exact job. Her second sentence was 'a house that needs to be packed up' and it never came back. The moment she finished the inventory he should have said: 'Stephanie, you mentioned the house still needs to be packed up — we can handle that for you at the same $104 per mover per hour plus materials at cost, and honestly on a three-stop day like this having the shed and the office pre-boxed is what keeps you at seven hours instead of nine. Do you want me to add a packing crew, or are you planning to pack it yourselves?' That one question either adds hours of billable packing or, if she declines, tells him the load-up estimate needs to move. Right now neither happened, and the 7-8 hour range is sitting on an inventory that includes a house nobody has agreed to pack. Second priority is the Save Your Ass speech, which he skipped on the most prep-friendly inventory imaginable — a loose shed, garage shelves, Christmas boxes, a container of cleaning supplies, patio furniture. The line he needed, right after the estimate: 'The single biggest thing you control here is prep. Anything loose in that shed — the Christmas decorations, the garden and garage odds and ends, the small stuff off the shelves — if that's boxed and staged by the door before we show up, you'll save real time, and time is the bill. And anything small enough to fit in your car, take a carload over yourself. Does that make sense?' Third, open with the agenda: 'Happy to help — I'll grab some details on what's moving and where, then walk you through pricing. Takes about ten or fifteen minutes. Sound good?' On an 18-minute three-stop call that one sentence buys patience for everything after it. Two smaller ones: say 'no hidden fees' and then land the On-Time Guarantee properly (if we miss the window we start discounting immediately, not just 'we won't be hours and hours late'), and use her name — twice in eighteen minutes on a returning customer is thin, especially when she handed him 'I've used you before' and got 'Oh, nice, okay' back. Methodology call worth flagging: I scored save_your_ass_hit as FALSE even though the section earned 4/10. He tied customer behavior to cost in general terms ('clear communication... does help be at four hours') and got the sense-check, but never gave a single pre-move-day action, so I did not count the differentiator as landed. If the tracking definition is looser than that, this one flips to true.
phone_presence_notes: Consultative and clearly engaged in the inventory work — 'I appreciate all those,' 'that's honestly easier to move when they don't,' and she volunteered 'I don't know you seem to remember better than I do' — but the warmth is task-warmth rather than personal, with heavy procedural filler ('Let's see here,' 'Alrighty,' 'Okay, gotcha' repeatedly), no warm-up, only two name uses, and a flat 'Oh, nice, okay, gotcha' when she revealed she was a returning customer; she still closed positive with 'Alright, great. Thank you so much.'
audio_review_reason: Transcript is materially garbled in places and speaker turns are interleaved out of sequence — Daniel's short acknowledgments appear stacked ahead of her answers, and several passages are clearly mis-transcribed ('Suck board the stand up surfboards', 'That is fix equipment still', 'panel board version table platies table thing', a stray 'Hey.'). The whole pricing/differentiator block reads as one long run, so pace, clarity and whether the No Worries / Meet Your Mover / On-Time sequence was delivered cleanly or rushed cannot be judged from text; audio also needed to confirm whether the packing question was asked and lost in the overlap.
